opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest lesson for me is that building a great technology and building a great company are two very different things. Coming from research, my instinct was always to focus on the technical problem: how do we make the compiler better, how do we get more performance out of the hardware. Those things matter, but in a startup you quickly learn that the technology is only one piece. You have to understand who your users really are, what problem they're actually willing to pay to solve, and how your work fits into their workflow. Sometimes the thing you're most proud of technically is not the thing customers care about most.

The second lesson is about people. In research you can make a lot of progress with a small group of students who share your passion. In a company you need people with very different skills: engineering, product, sales, operations. Learning to trust them, to communicate a shared vision, and to let others own important parts of the work was a big shift for me.

And finally, I learned to be more comfortable with uncertainty. The landscape in machine learning moves extremely fast. The hardware changes, the models change, and what the market needs can change within a year. You have to keep adapting while still holding on to a core belief about what you're building and why it matters. For me, that core belief has always been making machine learning more accessible and able to run efficiently everywhere. The startup experience actually sharpened that, and it influenced how I think about research and open source today: always staying close to real problems people face.

r001.rationale: The response says startup work requires a range of people skills beyond technical work, including trusting others, communicating a shared vision, and delegating ownership.

r002.rationale: The response mentions adapting as hardware and models change, but does not clearly state that startups must reinvent their technological approach as new technological eras emerge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest lesson, honestly, is that the hard part was never the technology. Coming from research, I spent years thinking the bottleneck was always the algorithm or the system design. You build something faster, you write the paper, and that's the win. With a company, the technology is maybe a third of it, and often not even the most important third.

What I underestimated is how much the work is really about people, both inside and outside. Inside, it's about finding people who can take ownership of a piece without needing you to specify everything, because in a startup there is never enough time to specify everything. Outside, it's about really listening to users. In research you optimize for a benchmark you chose. In a startup, the user chooses the benchmark, and it changes every few months. A lot of what we had to learn was to stop falling in love with our own abstraction and go ask what people were actually struggling with when they tried to deploy a model.

The second lesson is about focus. With open source, I was used to saying yes to a lot of directions, because the community can absorb that. A company can't. You have to pick one thing you are going to be undeniably good at, and say no to the rest, even when the rest is interesting. That was personally hard for me, because saying no to an interesting technical problem goes against every instinct I built as a researcher.

And the last thing, which sounds obvious but took me a while to really feel, is that speed of iteration matters more than being right the first time. I used to want to design the general solution upfront. Now I think you want the smallest thing that lets you learn something real from a user next week, and then you earn the right to generalize later.

r001.rationale: The candidate says startup work is largely about people inside and outside the company, and that technology is often not the most important part.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses changing user needs and iterating quickly, but does not state that startups must reinvent their technological approach as new technological eras emerge.

astra-6.text: I think the biggest lesson is to be willing to question your assumptions. You can be very excited about a technology, but building a company means figuring out whether it solves a problem that people actually care about. That requires listening, getting feedback early, and being willing to change direction. For me, the important thing is to stay committed to the problem while being flexible about the solution.

r001.rationale: It emphasizes listening to people, getting feedback, and solving problems they care about, beyond enthusiasm for the technology.

r002.rationale: It mentions changing direction and being flexible about the solution, but says nothing about reinventing a technological approach as new eras emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest lesson is to start with the problem people actually have. As engineers, we naturally get excited about technology, and we want to build something elegant. But in a startup, you have to ask: Who needs this? What is difficult for them today? And does what we’re building make that meaningfully better?

That means talking to users early and being willing to change your assumptions. You can have a long-term vision, but the way you get there has to evolve as you learn.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts engineers’ excitement about technology with the need to understand users’ problems and make their lives meaningfully better, identifying human needs as central to startup work.

r002.rationale: It says a startup’s approach should evolve as it learns, but does not state that startups must reinvent their technological approach as new technological eras emerge.
